title: When a practice stops fitting
hookLine: some practices are rafts, and some season ends: the Buddha's raft is for crossing over, not for carrying on your head
tomorrow: the Temple lay in ruins. what did a rabbi say would take its place?

cards: Clear out a closet and you'll find them: running shoes from one good spring, a journal with a few pages used. In one of his talks, the Buddha tells of a man who reaches a great flood. The near shore is dangerous.
The far shore is safe. No ferry, no bridge. So he gathers grass, sticks, branches and leaves, binds them into a raft, and paddles across with his hands and feet.
He makes it. He stands on the far bank, dripping, looking at the raft that saved him.

teach.b: Then he thinks: this raft was so useful. Shouldn't I lift it onto my head and carry it wherever I go? The Buddha asks his monks: would that be doing what should be done with a raft?
No. The man would pull it up onto the bank, or let it float off, and walk on. Then the Buddha names it.
The Dhamma, his teaching, is like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to. Even good teachings are to be let go of, he says, let alone what isn't good.
That's a striking thing for a teacher to say about his own teaching. Two details matter. The man doesn't let go in the middle of the river.

teach.h: LET GO ON THE FAR SHORE.
teach.b: You set the raft down on the far shore, after it has carried you. And he doesn't burn it or curse it.

teach.h: LEAVE IT ON THE BANK, WITH THANKS.
teach.b: He leaves it on the bank.

That's the Buddhist teaching of the raft: practices are means, not possessions, used fully while they carry you and set down when they've done their work. For a rule of your own, some practices are rafts.
A list, a page, a way of sitting that got you through one season. When you're across, you can set it down kindly, with thanks.

how: Buddhists know the simile of the raft from the Buddha's talk to his monks in the Majjhima Nikaya: the teaching is for crossing over, not for clinging to. On a personal rule, retiring a practice means setting it down deliberately, with thanks.

games.q: what does “when a practice stops fitting” mean?
o: a rule that you must quit anything once it gets hard
when a practice has carried you across and can be set down
the point when your old clothes no longer fit your body

p: not what should be done with a raft
for crossing over, not holding on to

s: the Buddha said to let go of the raft halfway across
the man sets it down on the far shore, after it has carried him.
the Buddha compared his own teaching to the raft
the Dhamma is for crossing over, not for holding on to.
the raft simile means teachings are useless
the raft saved the man's life. it's about how to hold it, not whether to build it.

games.q: your friend kept a strict no-sugar rule all through training for a race. the race is done and the rule now makes her anxious. what would the raft simile suggest?
o: it carried her across; she can set it down with thanks now.
keep it forever; dropping it would waste all that discipline.
she should have dropped it halfway through training.
games.why: the man left the raft on the far bank, after it had done its work, and walked on without it.

practice: Pick up a small object from a practice you've outgrown, or any small thing nearby, and feel its weight and texture in your hands. Then set it down gently beside you. Let your hands rest open for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: When a practice stops fitting: the moment a practice has carried you across, and you set it down with thanks, as with the Buddha's raft.

carryVoice: Your line: leave the raft. Set it down on the far bank, not midstream. Day 1677, across.

sources.ref: Alagaddupama Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 22 (the simile of the raft: for crossing over, not for grasping; let go even of good teachings)
